newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kremlin says general is suspended, not sacked.
newsitem.headline: Kremlin says general is suspended, not sacked.

text.p: The Kremlin blamed the Russian Defence Ministry on Tuesday for a continuing muddle over the removal of one of the country's most senior generals, accused of unspecified misconduct.

General Vladimir Semyonov, 56, commander of Russia's land forces, was sacked on Friday and his dismissal confirmed on Monday by the ministry, which accused him of "actions incompatible with his post".
But a spokesman for President Boris Yeltsin said on Tuesday the ministry had jumped the gun by telling the press Yeltsin had already signed a decree dismissing him.

Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had agreed to Defence Minister Igor Rodionov's request to suspend Semyonov but would not sign his dismissal decree until the accusations had been considered by a presidential committee on military appointments.
"This decree does not exist," Yastrzhembsky told a regular Kremlin briefing, pointedly avoiding any endorsement or repetition of the accusation of misconduct against Semyonov.
The defence ministry said Semyonov was sacked "for actions which discredit the honour and dignity of a serviceman and are incompatible with his post".
Yastrzhembsky said all questions about what he called "this strong formulation" should be addressed to the Defence Ministry. "Somebody was trying to anticipate events," he added.

General Semyonov told Izvestia newspaper he had been called in by Rodionov on Friday and told he was being sacked because of serious allegations about unspecified "commercial activities" of his wife, who works in the Moscow office of Rosvertol, a Russian helicopter manufacturer.
Russian commentators were sceptical of this argument but were mostly unable to come up with a better explanation for Semyonov's removal.

Interfax news agency quoted Semyonov as saying on Tuesday he had still not been presented with any concrete allegations of misconduct and disagreed strongly with the grounds given by the ministry for his removal.
He told Izvestia he would try to clear his name in court.
Once the pride of Soviet society, the army has seen morale plummet in recent years amid acute cash shortages and humiliation at the hands of separatists in Chechnya.
Rodionov, appointed in July on the recommendation of now ousted security supremo Alexander Lebed, has shown an uncertain political touch and has yet to impose his authority in the top ranks.
Semyonov was appointed commander of Soviet ground forces in 1991 after the dismissal of General Valentin Varennikov, a supporter of the unsuccessful coup against President Mikhail Gorbachev.
The following year, after the superpower collapsed and its armed forces were divided, he was appointed chief of Russian land forces.
